rows.evidence: The program and the detection equivalence are right: a positive objective gives nonnegative, nonzero net cash flows (and so does the netted position theta+ - theta-, whose cash flows are at least as large). The last sentence is false: 'Splitting a position into a purchase and a sale of the same asset only adds the spread to the cost, so the optimum never does it.' A same-asset round trip burns cash at the spread, and the program can use that to keep today's cash flow inside its box [0, 1] while it scales the state payoffs up, which raises the objective. Counterexample (positive prices, nonnegative payoffs; /tmp/claude-0/-home-claude/6f74c4e7-484a-542c-982f-ae21506915ed/scratchpad/L03-L04/scripts/r1_final.py, logs/r1_final.txt): two states, X = [[0.0116, 0.525], [0, 0.2118]], ask (1.5086, 2.8178), bid (1.1925, 2.4127). The LP optimum is 3.0, with theta+ = (435.667, 4.7214) and theta- = (563.1458, 0): asset 1 is bought and sold at once, today's cash flow is exactly 1 and the state payoffs are (1, 1). The best value without same-asset round trips is 2.4298. A random search over 3,000 small markets found 70 such cases (scripts/numchecks2.py).
rows.fix: Replace the last sentence of the R1 solution with: 'The optimum may buy and sell the same asset. The round trip burns cash at the spread, which lets the program keep today's cash flow inside its box while it scales the state payoffs up. R3, first bullet: 'a grid with the strikes as nodes captures everything the calls can distinguish, and Corollary 4.2's intervals on new payoffs depend only on that grid.' The second clause is false for a new payoff that is not linear between grid nodes (a digital between strikes, or a power payoff). The clause holds only for new payoffs that are piecewise linear with kinks at the nodes.

rows.location: course/modules/AP/AP1/L04.html figure lines 153-171 (svg.diagram, title 'Every SDF projects onto x star')
rows.evidence: Rendered at 360 px in light and dark (Chromium; /tmp/claude-0/-home-claude/6f74c4e7-484a-542c-982f-ae21506915ed/scratchpad/L03-L04/shots/L04_diagram_light.png, L04_diagram_dark.png): legible, colors from CSS tokens (accent-fill, ok-fill, bad-fill, stroke resolve differently per theme), source line present. The <desc> does not match the drawing. It says 'Dashed vertical segments, labelled epsilon and epsilon prime, drop from each' and 'The segments meet the line at right angles'. The SVG has one dashed line (x=180, y 40-165), one label 'ε' (at y=110, beside the m'-to-x* part rather than the m-to-x* segment it names), and no 'ε′' text. The caption says 'In more than three states the orthogonal complement has many dimensions'. The dimension of M^perp is S - dim M, not a function of S alone: three states and one payoff already give dimension 2 (Example 5.1), and four states with three payoffs give 1. The green (ok) and red (bad) fills for m and m' suggest a good/bad distinction the text never makes.
rows.fix: Draw the two residuals as separate labelled segments, e.g. m at (180,40) with ε on the full segment, and m' offset with its own dashed segment and 'ε′' label, both ending at x*. Or rewrite <desc> to describe exactly one dashed line through m' with one label ε. Use the same fill class for m and m'. Caption: 'When S - dim M > 1 the orthogonal complement has more than one dimension, and the SDFs fill an affine subspace x* + M^perp.'
